A limp is an uneven, irregular way of walking — where a person or animal cannot walk smoothly and puts noticeably more weight on one leg than the other.

Think of normal walking as a perfectly even rhythm — left, right, left, right — like a steady beat. A limp breaks that rhythm. One step is normal, but the other step is shorter, weaker, or accompanied by a dip of the body. The person appears to be slightly "sinking" or "bobbing" to one side with every step.

A limp happens when one leg (or foot) is painful, injured, weaker, or physically different from the other. Because it hurts or feels difficult to put full weight on that leg, the person instinctively protects it by shifting their weight quickly off it and onto the healthy leg. This is what creates the uneven movement you can see.

Common causes include:

  • A sprained ankle or sore knee
  • A broken bone that has healed but left weakness
  • Arthritis (painful, stiff joints)
  • A muscle or nerve problem
  • One leg being slightly shorter than the other

When someone walks with a limp:

  • Their body dips slightly downward on the side of the painful or weak leg
  • Their steps are not equal — one step is cautious and short, the other is more confident and full
  • Their walking has a noticeable rhythm break that your eye catches immediately
  • In more severe cases, they may swing the weak leg outward or drag it slightly
How It Is Used in Sentences

The noun "limp" almost always appears in a small set of very natural patterns. Here are the most important ones:

"walk with a limp" — This is the single most common way to use this word. It means the limp is an ongoing feature of how someone walks.

"Ever since the car accident, he walks with a limp."
"The old soldier walked with a noticeable limp."

"have a limp" — Similar to the above; it describes a limp as something a person possesses or carries.

"She has had a limp since childhood."
"Does the dog have a limp? It seems to be favouring one leg."

"develop a limp" — Used when a limp appears or begins, often after an injury or as a condition worsens.

"He developed a limp after the hiking accident."
"As her arthritis got worse, she developed a slight limp."

"a slight/faint limp" — Describes a limp that is barely noticeable.

"If you watch carefully, you can see she has a slight limp in her right leg."

"a pronounced/heavy/severe limp" — Describes a limp that is very obvious and significant.

"After the surgery, he was left with a pronounced limp."

A limp can be either temporary or permanent, and this distinction matters in real life:

  • A temporary limp comes and goes — for example, after twisting your ankle. Once the injury heals, the limp disappears. People often say someone is "limping" (verb) in this case, but you might also say they have a limp for now.
  • A permanent limp is long-lasting or lifelong, often due to a serious injury, surgery, or a physical condition that doesn't go away. This is when people most naturally say someone walks with a limp or has a limp, implying it is a fixed part of how they move.

The word applies equally to animals, and is used in exactly the same way:

"The vet noticed a limp in the horse's front leg."
"Our dog came home with a limp — we think he stepped on something sharp."

If you ever forget the meaning, picture this: an old pirate captain — one leg injured from battle — walking across a ship's deck. Every time he steps on the bad leg, his body drops slightly to that side, and he quickly lifts off it and lands on the good leg. That uneven, dipping, protective walk? That is a limp.
